media.title: How many leaps before the cat catches the mouse?
media.context: Finding Common Ground. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: A cat chases a mouse that starts forty eight feet ahead, and each leap of the cat is seven feet against five feet for the mouse. The board finds how much the cat gains in one leap, then how many such gains fill the head start. Keeko's doubt is that the two leaps should be added.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: both run the same way, so the cat closes the gap by the difference of the two leaps, and the head start is divided by that gain. Watch for children who add the two leap lengths.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

source_video_walkthrough.title: How many leaps before the cat catches the mouse?
items: A cat chases a mouse that has a head start of 48 feet. The c
source_video_walkthrough.intent: The child can take away and divide, but has not yet seen a chase as a gap that shrinks by the same amount each leap.

interaction_points.prompt: In how many leaps does the cat catch the mouse?
covers: A cat chases a mouse that has a head start of 48 feet. The c

source: A cat chases a mouse that has a head start of 48 feet. The c
video_script.why: The child can take away and divide, but has not yet seen a chase as a gap that shrinks by the same amount each leap.
video_script.substitution: The head start is the gap, and each leap shrinks the gap by the cat's leap less the mouse's leap.
video_script.anchor: a cat and a mouse on a straight line, the mouse forty eight feet ahead
video_script.wrong_move: adds the two leap lengths instead of taking the smaller from the larger
video_script.payoff_line: The cat catches the mouse in twenty four leaps

final_answer.spoken: twenty four leaps

maths_rules: both run the same way, so in one leap the cat gains 7 - 5 = 2 feet
the gap of 48 feet closes by 2 feet each leap, so leaps = 48 / 2 = 24
check: the cat runs 24 x 7 = 168 feet; the mouse runs 48 + 24 x 5 = 48 + 120 = 168 feet; they are equal
wrong idea: 7 + 5 = 12 and 48 / 12 = 4 leaps

media.title: How do we add one sixth and one fourth?
media.context: Finding Common Ground. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Two fractions with different bottom numbers sit on one board. The lowest common multiple of the bottom numbers turns both into pieces of the same size, and then the tops are added. Keeko's doubt is that the tops and the bottoms can each be added straight away.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: fractions are added only after both are changed to the lowest common multiple of their bottom numbers; then the tops are added and the bottom stays. Watch for children who add the tops and the bottoms separately.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

source_video_walkthrough.title: How do we add one sixth and one fourth?
items: Add 1/6 and 1/4 using the LCM of the denominators.
source_video_walkthrough.intent: The child can build the lowest common multiple from primes but has not yet used it to add fractions.

interaction_points.prompt: What is one sixth plus one fourth?
covers: Add 1/6 and 1/4 using the LCM of the denominators.

source: Add 1/6 and 1/4 using the LCM of the denominators.
video_script.why: The child can build the lowest common multiple from primes but has not yet used it to add fractions.
video_script.substitution: The lowest common multiple of the bottom numbers is the smallest size of piece that both fractions can be changed into.
video_script.anchor: two strips of equal length, one cut into six pieces and one cut into four pieces
video_script.wrong_move: adds the tops and adds the bottoms separately
video_script.payoff_line: The sum is five twelfths

final_answer.spoken: five twelfths

video_script.fraction_reading: 1/6 is one sixth, 1/4 is one fourth, 2/12 is two twelfths, 3/12 is three twelfths, 5/12 is five twelfths, 2/10 is two tenths
maths_rules: 6 = 2 x 3 and 4 = 2 x 2; most 2s is two, most 3s is one, so LCM = 2 x 2 x 3 = 12
5/12 is bigger than 1/4 = 3/12 and than 1/6 = 2/12, as a sum should be
wrong idea: (1 + 1)/(6 + 4) = 2/10, and 2/10 = 0.2 is smaller than 1/4 = 0.25
video_script.design: Two strips of the same length cut into sixths and fourths, then both cut into twelfths. Assumes the lowest common multiple from primes. Keeko's doubt: add tops and bottoms separately.

<bookmark mark='m2'/>A sixth and a fourth are different sizes, so we cannot add them yet.

concepts.concept_name: End of chapter Figure it Out, Q8

content.text:
End of chapter Figure it Out, Q8: Find the smallest number that is divisible by 3, 4, 5 and 7, but leaves a remainder of 10 when divided by 11.
1. A number divisible by 3, 4, 5 and 7 is a multiple of their LCM, 3 × 4 × 5 × 7 = 420.
2. Multiples of 420: 420, 840, 1260, 1680, 2100.
3. Check remainders on division by 11: 420 gives 2, 840 gives 4, 1260 gives 6, 1680 gives 8, 2100 gives 10.
4. So the smallest such number is 2100.
Answer: 2100

concepts.concept_name: End of chapter Figure it Out, Q9

content.text:
End of chapter Figure it Out, Q9: Children are playing 'Fire in the Mountain'. When the number 6 was called out, no one got out. When the number 9 was called out, no one got out. But when the number 10 was called out, some people got out. How many children could have been playing initially? (a) 72 (b) 90 (c) 45 (d) 3 (e) 36 (f) None of these
1. No one got out on 6 and on 9, so the children split into groups of 6 and of 9 with none left over.
2. So the number is a common multiple of 6 and 9, that is a multiple of their LCM, 18.
3. Some got out on 10, so the number is not a multiple of 10.
4. Multiples of 18 among the options: 72 and 36 (90 is also a multiple of 10, so nobody would be out on 10).
5. So 72 and 36 fit.
Answer: (a) 72 and (e) 36

concepts.concept_name: End of chapter Figure it Out, Q10

content.text:
End of chapter Figure it Out, Q10: Tick the correct statement(s). The LCM of two different prime numbers (m, n) can be: (a) Less than both numbers (b) In between the two numbers (c) Greater than both numbers (d) Less than m × n (e) Greater than m × n
1. Two different primes are co-prime, so their LCM is their product m × n.
2. m × n is bigger than both m and n, since each is at least 2.
3. So (c) is true, and (a), (b), (d) and (e) are false.
Answer: (c) Greater than both numbers

concepts.concept_name: End of chapter Figure it Out, Q11

content.text:
End of chapter Figure it Out, Q11: A dog is chasing a rabbit that has a head start of 150 feet. It jumps 9 feet every time the rabbit jumps 7 feet. In how many leaps does the dog catch up with the rabbit?
1. In each leap the dog gains 9 − 7 = 2 feet.
2. It must gain 150 feet, so it needs 150 ÷ 2 = 75 leaps.
3. Check: the dog goes 75 × 9 = 675 feet and the rabbit 150 + 75 × 7 = 675 feet.
Answer: 75 leaps

2. It must gain 150 feet, so it needs 150 ÷ 2 = 75 leaps.
3. Check: the dog goes 75 × 9 = 675 feet and the rabbit 150 + 75 × 7 = 675 feet.
Answer: 75 leaps

concepts.concept_name: End of chapter Figure it Out, Q12

content.text:
End of chapter Figure it Out, Q12: What is the smallest number that is a multiple of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10? Do you remember the answer from Grade 6, Chapter 5?
1. The smallest such number is the LCM of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 and 10.
2. The highest powers: 2 three times (from 8), 3 twice (from 9), 5 once (from 5 and 10).
3. LCM = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 = 360.
Answer: 360

concepts.concept_name: End of chapter Figure it Out, Q13

content.text:
End of chapter Figure it Out, Q13: Here is a problem posed by the ancient Indian Mathematician Mahaviracharya (850 C.E.). Add together 8/15, 1/20, 7/36, 11/63 and 1/21. What do you get? How can we find this sum efficiently?
1. The LCM of the denominators 15, 20, 36, 63 and 21 gives the lowest common denominator.
2. 15 = 3 × 5, 20 = 2 × 2 × 5, 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3, 63 = 3 × 3 × 7, 21 = 3 × 7.
3. LCM = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 7 = 1260.
4. 8/15 = 672/1260, 1/20 = 63/1260, 7/36 = 245/1260, 11/63 = 220/1260, 1/21 = 60/1260.
5. 672 + 63 + 245 + 220 + 60 = 1260, so the sum is 1260/1260 = 1.
Answer: The sum is 1

maths_rules: 3, 4 = 2 x 2, 5 and 7 share no prime, so LCM = 3 x 4 x 5 x 7 = 420
420 = 11 x 38 + 2, since 11 x 38 = 418; remainder 2
5 x 420 = 11 x 190 + 10, since 11 x 190 = 2090 and 2090 + 10 = 2100; remainder 10, which is the clue
so the smallest such number is 5 x 420 = 2100
check: 420 = 3 x 140 = 4 x 105 = 5 x 84 = 7 x 60, so 2100 is divisible by 3, 4, 5 and 7

media.description: In a game of Fire in the Mountain no one gets out on two calls but some children get out on a third. The board finds the lowest common multiple of the first two numbers, keeps the options that are its multiples, and then uses the third call to drop any option that ten divides.

media.description: The board takes two different prime numbers, finds their lowest common multiple from their prime factors, and compares it with each prime and with their multiplication. It rules out the false statements one by one and checks the result with two small primes.

media.description: A dog chases a rabbit that starts one hundred and fifty feet ahead, and each leap of the dog is nine feet against seven feet for the rabbit. content.text:

steps: Predict first: which would you use to find when two cycles meet, and which to cut equal pieces?
Choose a method: list for small numbers, prime factorisation for bigger ones, the division ladder when both values are wanted.
Check with HCF × LCM = the product of the two numbers.

content.text:
Worked example: Find the HCF and LCM of 42 and 70, and check with the product rule.
1. 42 = 2 × 3 × 7 and 70 = 2 × 5 × 7.
2. Minimum counts: 2 once, 7 once, so HCF = 2 × 7 = 14.
3. Maximum counts: 2, 3, 5 and 7 once each, so LCM = 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 = 210.
4. Check: 14 × 210 = 2940 and 42 × 70 = 2940.
Answer: HCF 14, LCM 210, and 14 × 210 = 2940 = 42 × 70

content.text:
Worked example: Find the HCF and LCM of 8 and 15, of 7 and 21, and of 12 and 13 without long working.
1. 8 and 15 are co-prime: HCF 1 and LCM 8 × 15 = 120.
2. 7 is a factor of 21: HCF 7 and LCM 21.
3. 12 and 13 are consecutive, so co-prime: HCF 1 and LCM 12 × 13 = 156.
Answer: (8, 15): 1 and 120; (7, 21): 7 and 21; (12, 13): 1 and 156

source_video_walkthrough.title: How do we find the HCF and LCM of 42 and 70?
items: Find the HCF and LCM of 42 and 70, and check with the product rule.
source_video_walkthrough.intent: The child can find each of the two from primes, and now finds both together and sees how they link to the numbers.

interaction_points.prompt: What are these two numbers?
covers: Find the HCF and LCM of 42 and 70, and check with the product rule.

source: Find the HCF and LCM of 42 and 70, and check with the product rule.
video_script.why: The child can find each of the two from primes, and now finds both together and sees how they link to the numbers.
video_script.substitution: The fewest copies of each prime make the highest common factor, the most copies make the lowest common multiple, and the two together use every prime of both numbers.
video_script.anchor: two number cards, forty two and seventy, each broken into a block of primes
video_script.wrong_move: multiplies the two numbers and calls the result the lowest common multiple, counting the shared primes twice
video_script.payoff_line: The highest common factor is fourteen and the lowest common multiple is two hundred and ten

final_answer.spoken: the highest common factor is fourteen and the lowest common multiple is two hundred and ten

maths_rules: fewest copies: 2 once, 7 once, 3 and 5 missing from one number; HCF = 2 x 7 = 14
most copies: 2, 3, 5 and 7 once each; LCM = 2 x 3 x 5 x 7 = 210
check: HCF x LCM = (2 x 7) x (2 x 3 x 5 x 7) = 2 x 2 x 3 x 5 x 7 x 7, and 42 x 70 = (2 x 3 x 7) x (2 x 5 x 7) = 2 x 2 x 3 x 5 x 7 x 7
wrong idea: 42 x 70 = 2940 counts the shared 2 and 7 twice; 2940 / 210 = 14, which is the HCF
video_script.design: Two number cards broken into prime blocks, the shared primes overlapping. The highest common factor takes the fewest copies, the lowest common multiple the most. Keeko's doubt: the lowest common multiple is the two numbers multiplied.

media.title: Can we find the HCF and LCM of a pair at a glance?
media.context: Finding Common Ground. Concept video: one solved example from the book, shown after the concept that uses its idea. It ends when Keeko raises a hand with a doubt. PLACEHOLDER: scripted to docs/28, not rendered yet.
media.description: Three pairs of numbers are looked at for a pattern: no shared prime, one number a factor of the other, and numbers that follow each other. Each pattern gives the highest common factor and the lowest common multiple without long working. Keeko's doubt is that the bigger number of a pair is the highest common factor.
media.teaching_notes: One idea: spot the pattern first. Co-prime numbers have a highest common factor of one and a lowest common multiple equal to their multiplication, and when one number is a factor of the other, the smaller is the highest common factor and the bigger is the lowest common multiple. Watch for children who call the bigger number the highest common factor.
media.instructions_for_student: When the video says think and tell, say your answer out loud. Then watch how the book's example is solved.

video_script.why: The child can find the highest common factor and lowest common multiple from primes and now learns to see the answer from the pattern of the pair.
video_script.substitution: A pair that shares no prime gives a highest common factor of one and a lowest common multiple equal to the multiplication, and a pair where one number divides the other gives the smaller number as the highest common factor and the bigger as the lowest common multiple.

final_answer.spoken: eight and fifteen give one and one hundred and twenty, seven and twenty one give seven and twenty one, and twelve and thirteen give one and one hundred and fifty six

maths_rules: 8 = 2 x 2 x 2 and 15 = 3 x 5 share no prime, so they are co-prime: HCF = 1 and LCM = 8 x 15 = 120
21 = 3 x 7, so 7 is a factor of 21: HCF = 7 and LCM = 21
12 and 13 differ by 1; a number that divides both divides 13 - 12 = 1, so HCF = 1 and LCM = 12 x 13 = 156
wrong idea: 21 does not divide 7, so it is not a common factor

marks.m3: HCF = 1 and LCM = 8 x 15 are written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, look at eight and fifteen. Eight is two times two times two, and fifteen is three times five.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>They share no prime, so they are co-prime.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The highest common factor is one, and the lowest common multiple is eight times fifteen.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: 7 and 21. 21 = 3 x 7, so 7 is a factor of 21. HCF = 7. LCM = 21

marks.m1: 21 = 3 x 7 is written and the 7 inside it is circled
marks.m2: 7 is a factor of 21 is written
marks.m3: HCF = 7 and LCM = 21 are written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, look at seven and twenty one. Twenty one is three times seven.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Seven is a factor of twenty one, so twenty one already holds all of seven.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The highest common factor is seven, and the lowest common multiple is twenty one.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: 12 and 13. The gap is 13 - 12 = 1. A number that divides both divides the gap 1. So they are co-prime. HCF = 1. LCM = 12 x 13

marks.m1: 12 and 13 are written with the gap 13 - 12 = 1 between them
marks.m2: a number that divides both divides the gap 1 is written
marks.m3: the word co-prime is written
marks.m4: HCF = 1 and LCM = 12 x 13 are written

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, look at twelve and thirteen. They follow each other, so the gap between them is one.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>A number that divides both must also divide the gap, which is one.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Only one does, so they are co-prime.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>The highest common factor is one, and the lowest common multiple is twelve times thirteen.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: check. HCF divides both numbers. LCM is a multiple of both. HCF x LCM = product: 1 x (8 x 15) = 8 x 15; 7 x 21 = 7 x 21; 1 x (12 x 13) = 12 x 13

marks.m1: the heading check is written
marks.m2: each HCF is joined by arrows to both numbers of its pair
marks.m3: each LCM is joined by arrows to both numbers of its pair
marks.m4: the three product lines are written with ticks

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, check each answer.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Each highest common factor divides both numbers in its pair.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Each lowest common multiple is a multiple of both numbers.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>In each pair, the highest common factor times the lowest common multiple equals the product of the pair.

marks.m1: 8 x 15 turns into 120 and the first pair is boxed with HCF 1, LCM 120
marks.m2: the second pair is boxed with HCF 7, LCM 21
marks.m3: 12 x 13 turns into 156 and the third pair is boxed with HCF 1, LCM 156

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Eight and fifteen give one and one hundred and twenty.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Seven and twenty one give seven and twenty one.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Twelve and thirteen give one and one hundred and fifty six. In each answer the highest common factor comes first.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the pair 7 and 21

marks.m1: Keeko raises a hand

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: a doubt bubble says HCF of 7 and 21 = 21; a check shows 21 divides 21 but not 7; the bubble is struck through and HCF = 7 glows

marks.m1: the doubt bubble with HCF = 21 appears
marks.m2: a check shows 21 divides 21 but 7 divided by 21 is not a whole number
marks.m3: the bubble is struck through and HCF = 7 glows

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks twenty one is the highest common factor of seven and twenty one. It is the bigger number.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But a common factor must divide both numbers. Twenty one divides itself, but it does not divide seven.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>A factor can never be bigger than the smaller number, so the highest common factor is seven.

concepts.concept_name: What we found about HCF and LCM

content.text:
Summary
Last year, we looked at common multiples, and common factors, and were also introduced to the amazing world of primes!
In this chapter, we learnt a method to find the prime factorisation of a number.
Finding all the factors of a number from its prime factorisation is easy but quite tedious, we have to list every possible subpart!
The Highest Common Factor (HCF) is the highest among all the common factors of a group of numbers. Every common factor is contained in the prime factorisation of the number. To find the HCF, we include the minimum number of occurrences of each prime across the prime factorisation of all the numbers.
The Lowest Common Multiple (LCM) is the lowest among all the common multiples of a group of numbers. Every common multiple contains the prime factorisation of the numbers. To find the LCM, we include the highest number of occurrences of each prime across the prime factorisations of all the numbers.
We explored more about HCF and LCM; we discovered related properties and patterns when numbers are consecutive, even, co-prime, etc.
We learnt a procedure to get both the HCF and the LCM at the same time! We also saw how to make this even quicker!
We learned some terms that are used when discussing mathematics, such as 'conjecture' and 'generalisation'.
The largest prime found so far has 4,10,24,320 digits! It was discovered on October 12, 2024.

objectives.objective_text: Students list the factors of 12 and of 16, pick out the common factors, and explain why the largest common factor gives the fewest square tiles for the 12 ft by 16 ft room.
Students define the HCF, also called the GCD, count the 4 ft tiles needed for the room, and check that allowing fractional tile sides does not make a larger tile possible.
Students list the factors of two numbers, circle the common ones and name the HCF for several pairs, checking the largest common factor against a picture of squares on a rectangle.
Students list the factors of 84 and 108, find their common factors, choose the weight giving the fewest bags, and count the bags from each farm.
Students find the largest equal bag weight for two quantities by listing the factors of each, keeping the common factors and choosing the greatest.
Students find the longest jump from 0 that lands on both treasures for four number pairs, by listing the jump sizes that land on each number.
Students compare the longest jump with the HCF for each pair, explain why a jump landing on both numbers is a common factor, and say why the longest such jump must be the HCF.
Students find the longest jump that lands on both of two treasure numbers by listing the factors of each number and choosing the greatest common factor.
Students explain why listing factors becomes slow and unreliable for numbers like 30, 50, 28 and 42, and decide whether a number is prime or composite by counting its factors.
Students decide whether a number is prime or composite by counting its factors, and say why 1 and numbers such as 91 need extra care.
Students split 90 into primes along different routes, see the same primes appear in a different order, and state the prime factorisation of a prime number.
Students read the factor figures for 105 and 30, use the division method with a vertical bar, and find the prime factorisation of 1200 by division.
Students split numbers into primes with a factor tree and with the division method, check that the product of the primes returns the number, and see different routes meet at the same primes.
Students split 840 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 into two groups of primes to show a number is a factor, and say why 14 and 8 are factors but 27 is not.
Students list all the factors of 225 by combining its primes one, two, three and four at a time, add 1, and check the list against a direct count.
Students test the claim that a larger number always has a longer prime factorisation, disprove it with 96 and 121, and name a conjecture and a counterexample.
Students build the full factor list of a number from the subparts of its prime factorisation, in order, and check that no factor is missing and none is repeated.
Students write the prime factorisations of 45 and 75, list the subparts common to both, and read off the common factors and the HCF.
Students list all the subparts common to 112 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 7 and 84 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7, and name the common factors and the HCF.
Students show that 96 and 275 share no prime, conclude that 1 is their only common factor and so their HCF, and say what such numbers are called.
Students write two prime factorisations side by side, pick out the common subparts, and list the common factors and the HCF, including pairs with no common prime.
Students identify the common primes of 30 and 72, count how many times each occurs in each number, and build the HCF by taking the minimum count of each.
Students find the HCF of 225 and 750 by minimum counts, and extend the same method to three numbers by keeping only primes that appear in all of them.
Students build the HCF prime by prime from the minimum count in each factorisation, for two or three numbers, and test why composite-looking factorisations can hide common primes.
Students list the multiples of 6 and 8, pick the toran lengths common to both lists, and identify 24 cm as the shortest toran both can stitch.
Students define the LCM as the lowest common multiple, say why 24 is the LCM of 6 and 8, and explain why a largest common multiple cannot exist.
Students lay strips of two lengths side by side to find the shortest equal toran, list common multiples on two rulers, and confirm that the LCM is the first match.
Students list the multiples of 7 and of 10 as days, find the first day common to both, and name 70 days as the LCM of 7 and 10.
Students play Idli-Vada for four pairs, find the first number called out for both, and explain why this number is always the LCM of the two numbers.
Students list the multiples of two repeating schedules, find the first day both repeat, and explain why that day is the LCM of the two numbers.
Students compare 36 with its multiple 648, see that the multiple holds all the primes of the number, and build the LCM of 14 and 35 as the smallest number holding both factorisations.
Students build the LCM of 96 and 360 prime by prime using the maximum number of occurrences, and extend the method to three numbers.
Students build the LCM prime by prime from the maximum count in each factorisation, for two or three numbers, and check that every number divides the result.
Students find pairs whose HCF is one of the two numbers, state that one number must be a factor of the other, and write this pattern in algebra with n and 5n.
Students try examples for consecutive even, consecutive odd, consecutive and co-prime pairs, and explain why each HCF and LCM pattern holds using common factors and primes.
Students generate many pairs of a chosen type, read the HCF and LCM for each, and state and explain a general statement for consecutive, even, odd, multiple and co-prime pairs.
Students double pairs of numbers, see that the HCF also doubles, and explain this using the extra prime 2 that both numbers gain and that joins the largest common subpart.
Students find the HCF of two multiples of 14 and of four more pairs sharing a common multiplier, and say when the HCF equals the common multiplier.
Students scale a pair by a common multiplier, explain why the HCF scales with it, and decide whether the HCF equals the multiplier by testing whether the remaining factors are co-prime.
Students explain the common division steps for 84 and 180, see that the divisors multiply to the HCF, and use the steps to find the HCF in two more cases.
Students find the LCM from the division steps by multiplying the divisors with the last row, and explain why this contains both numbers and is the smallest such number.
Students check Guna's and Anshu's faster division steps for 300 and 150 and for 630 and 770, explain why any common divisor works, and use the faster steps on two new pairs.
Students climb the common division method for pairs of numbers, choosing any common divisor each step, and read the HCF from the divisors and the LCM from the divisors with the last row.
Students compare the LCM with the product for several pairs and explain why the LCM is never greater, because the product is itself a common multiple.
Students find the LCM of 105 and 95, see the product is the LCM times the HCF, test three more pairs, and state HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers.
Students explain HCF × LCM = product by splitting each prime between the HCF and the LCM, and show with a counter-example that the rule fails for three numbers.
Students compute the HCF, the LCM and the product for pairs, check HCF × LCM, use it to find a missing value, and test the rule on three numbers.
Students read a situation, decide whether it asks to split into equal pieces or to find when events meet, and so choose the HCF or the LCM, then compute it for two stories.
Students find the HCF and LCM of numbers given as products of primes, taking minimum and maximum counts, and say why a product of primes is a multiple or factor of another.
Students read each problem, decide whether it asks for the HCF or the LCM, solve it from prime factorisations, and check that the answer suits the story.
Students find the smallest number divisible by several numbers that leaves a given remainder when divided by another, and the number of leaps for a chaser who gains a fixed distance each leap.
Students use the LCM of the denominators as a common denominator, convert each fraction, and add them efficiently.
Students solve remainder, chase, fraction-sum and prime-LCM problems, choosing HCF or LCM themselves, and check each answer against the story.
Students decide whether a problem needs the HCF or the LCM, choose listing, prime factorisation or the common division method as suits the numbers, and check with HCF × LCM = product.
Students handle co-prime pairs, one number a factor of the other, and consecutive numbers quickly, and solve a closing problem that combines splitting and meeting.
Students solve mixed questions on common factors, primes, HCF, LCM, patterns, the common division method and applications, choosing the idea and the method that suit each question.
Students restate how the HCF and LCM come from prime factorisations, recall the tile, toran and sweet shop stories, and name the patterns and the efficient procedure found in this chapter.
